raw_text:
### Introduction and Pathophysiology
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major cardiovascular challenge, increasing the risk of ischemic stroke five-fold. While oral anticoagulation (OAC) is the standard therapy, bleeding risks and non-compliance limit its long-term use. Since over 90% of cardioembolic thrombi in non-valvular AF originate in the left atrial appendage (LAA), percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has emerged as an effective mechanical alternative.

### Clinical Evidence and Evolving Devices
The clinical efficacy of endovascular LAAC was first established in the vitamin K antagonist (VKA) era. The landmark PROTECT AF [1] and PREVAIL [2] randomized clinical trials compared the first-generation WATCHMAN device (Boston Scientific) with warfarin. A patient-level meta-analysis of both trials with 5-year follow-up confirmed that LAAC provided comparable stroke prevention to warfarin, with a 30% reduction in all-cause mortality and an 80% reduction in hemorrhagic stroke [3].

Subsequent iterations of endovascular devices have sought to optimize closure and reduce complications. The AMPLATZER Amulet (Abbott) utilizes a dual-seal "disc-and-lobe" design. In the AMULET IDE trial, the Amulet device was shown to be non-inferior to the first-generation WATCHMAN for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, or cardiovascular death, with higher rates of complete LAA occlusion [4]. The long-term durability of these results was recently confirmed in the 5-year follow-up of the AMULET IDE trial [5]. Concurrently, the next-generation WATCHMAN FLX device, featuring a closed-end design and more anchors, demonstrated exceptional safety and a 100% rate of effective closure in the PINNACLE FLX trial [6], with sustained efficacy and low stroke rates through 2 years [7].

### Transition to the DOAC Era
As direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) became the pharmacological standard, trials began comparing LAAC directly to these safer agents. The PRAGUE-17 trial randomized high-risk AF patients to LAAC (using predominantly Amulet or WATCHMAN) versus DOAC therapy, demonstrating non-inferiority for the primary net clinical outcome at 2 years [8], which remained consistent at 4 years of follow-up [9]. More recently, the landmark OPTION trial demonstrated that in patients undergoing catheter ablation for AF, LAAC with the WATCHMAN FLX device was non-inferior to OAC for the primary efficacy composite of death, stroke, or systemic embolism at 3 years, and was superior in reducing non-procedural bleeding [10]. The large-scale CHAMPION-AF trial further expanded these findings, showing that WATCHMAN FLX was non-inferior to DOAC therapy in an anticoagulation-eligible population [11]. However, the CLOSURE-AF trial, which enrolled exceptionally high-risk patients with relative contraindications to OAC, failed to demonstrate the non-inferiority of LAAC to medical therapy, emphasizing the critical role of patient selection and procedural safety in fragile cohorts [12].

### Real-World Registries and Clinical Guidelines
Prospective registries have confirmed the high implant success and safety of LAAC in clinical practice. The EWOLUTION registry demonstrated a 98.5% deployment success rate with low peri-procedural complications [13] and sustained clinical benefits at 1 year [14]. Similarly, the Amplatzer Amulet Global Observational Registry highlighted low periprocedural complication rates in real-world practice [15], with excellent stroke prevention and low device-related thrombus (DRT) rates at 1 year [16]. In the United States, the National Cardiovascular Data Registry (NCDR) LAAO Registry, which analyzed over 38,000 procedures, confirmed high procedural success (98.3%) and a low rate of in-hospital major adverse events [17].

Based on this robust evidence, the joint SCAI/HRS expert consensus statement supports LAAC as a viable alternative to OAC in patients with non-valvular AF at high thromboembolic risk who have an appropriate rationale to avoid long-term anticoagulation [18]. This is reflected in the 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS guidelines [19] and the 2024 ESC guidelines [20], which assign a Class IIb recommendation for LAAC in patients with contraindications to long-term OAC. Furthermore, the early ASAP study had previously demonstrated the feasibility of LAAC in patients with absolute contraindications to OAC who were managed with dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) post-procedure [21]. Head-to-head comparisons of the two leading devices have also been performed; the SWISS-APERO randomized trial demonstrated superior complete closure rates with the Amulet device compared to the WATCHMAN at 1 year [22], although 3-year clinical outcomes showed comparable rates of stroke, death, and major bleeding between the two cohorts [23].

### Complications and Procedural Optimization
The principal challenges of percutaneous LAAC are peri-device leak (PDL) and device-related thrombus (DRT). Analysis of the PROTECT AF and PREVAIL trials over 5 years revealed that while minor PDL (≤5 mm) is common, any degree of residual patency is associated with a higher long-term thromboembolic risk [24], a finding supported by real-world data from the NCDR registry [25]. To mitigate these issues, optimizing post-procedural antithrombotic regimens is essential. While traditional protocols used warfarin or DAPT, recent evidence suggests that direct oral anticoagulation (DOAC) monotherapy may reduce DRT compared to DAPT without increasing major bleeding [26]. Simard et al. identified specific clinical and anatomical predictors of DRT, including prior stroke, LAA size, and device undersizing, highlighting the need for individualized antithrombotic therapy [27].

Procedural success relies heavily on advanced imaging. While transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) remains the standard, the prospective ICE LAA study showed that intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) is a safe and effective alternative to guide WATCHMAN FLX implantation, eliminating the need for general anesthesia [28]. Additionally, expert recommendations emphasize the role of pre-procedural cardiac computed tomography (CCTA) for precise device sizing and anatomical characterization [29]. Finally, regarding post-implant regimens, an NCDR registry analysis showed that DAPT is a safe and comparable alternative to OAC during the initial 45-day post-LAAC healing phase, especially in patients with high bleeding risks [30].

### Conclusion
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure is a highly effective, evidence-based alternative to oral anticoagulation for stroke prevention in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation. Continual improvements in device design, pre-procedural planning, and post-procedural antithrombotic management will further refine the safety and efficacy of this rapidly growing structural intervention.
